title: Minerals
intro: A mineral is a natural, solid, crystal 'building block' of rocks. Learn what counts as a mineral, how atoms are arranged inside it, how the silica tetrahedron builds the silicate minerals, and how to tell minerals apart (colour, streak, luster, hardness, cleavage). Key idea: the way the atoms are packed and bonded controls the crystal shape, the hardness AND the cleavage.

learningObjectives.text: Define a mineral using the five required criteria.
Distinguish minerals from glass, synthetic materials, and amber using the mineral criteria.
Explain how atoms, chemical bonds, isotopes, and polymorphs relate to mineral properties.
Describe crystal growth and distinguish the six crystal systems.
Explain the main processes by which minerals form.
Identify minerals using color, streak, and luster.
Use the Mohs scale to compare mineral hardness.
Distinguish cleavage from fracture using mineral breakage patterns.
Use special physical properties to identify minerals.
Identify the major elements in Earth and its crust.
Describe the silica tetrahedron and compare the main silicate structures.
Recognize common rock-forming minerals and distinguish silicates from nonsilicates.

boxes.text: Why 'crystalline' matters: the repeating atom pattern is what gives a mineral a fixed shape and fixed properties (hardness, cleavage). Without the pattern there is no consistent property set to identify.
Checklist trick: N-I-S-C-C = Natural, Inorganic, Solid, Crystalline, Chemical formula (definite). If one letter fails, it is not a mineral.
Do not say a mineral can never touch life: biogenic minerals exist (see next section).

steps.title: The definition
bullets: A mineral is a **naturally occurring, inorganic** element or compound with a **periodically repeating arrangement of atoms** and a characteristic chemical composition. That gives it distinctive physical properties.
Another wording: a mineral is an element or chemical compound that is **crystalline** and formed by **geologic processes**.

steps.title: Ice is a mineral
bullets: Ice is a mineral: it is natural, it is solid, and its feathery crystals show an ordered atom structure.
Most solid inorganic materials are crystalline: the atoms sit in neat rows like soldiers. In a **glass** the atoms are jumbled with no order.

steps.title: The five checks
bullets: In one line: minerals are naturally occurring, (mostly) inorganic **crystalline solids** formed by geologic processes, with a **definite chemical composition**.
So the 5 checks are: natural, inorganic (mostly), solid, **crystalline** (atoms in a repeating pattern), and a **definite chemical composition**. Formed by geologic processes ties them together.
This giant red crystal is the Alma King rhodocrosite (MnCO3). Its fixed formula shows what a definite chemical composition means.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Mineral names come from people, places, things, composition, physical properties or other languages. Stilbite comes from the Greek for 'to shine'.
Minerals matter to people: malachite is a copper mineral, and copper ores give us copper pots and electrical wire.

sections.title: What is NOT a mineral (glass, synthetic, amber)

boxes.text: Why is amber not a mineral? It comes from living trees (organic) and is not a crystal with a repeating atom pattern. Quartz, olivine, garnet and diamond are all natural crystalline solids with definite compositions.
Mineral test in one breath: 'Was it made by nature, not by a lab, and not a jumble?' Lab = synthetic. Jumble = glass. Plant or animal goo = organic.
Practice-midterm Q12: obsidian is the NOT-a-mineral answer. Ice, halite, native gold and quartz are all minerals. 'It is a rock' is not the reason; the reason is no crystal structure (glass).

steps.title: Glass breaks in curves
bullets: **Glass has no crystal order**: obsidian is natural volcanic glass. Its atoms have no repeating pattern, so it is not a mineral.
Glass breaks with **conchoidal fracture** (a smooth, curved, shell-like surface). A stone tool made of obsidian shows this.

steps.title: Biogenic minerals
bullets: **Biogenic minerals** are formed by living things, such as the aragonite in a blue mussel shell. They are a **special case**.
Normal formation: freezing from a melt, precipitation from solution, or chemical reaction.

steps.title: Which one is not a mineral?
bullets: Quartz, olivine, garnet and diamond are all minerals. **Amber** is the one that is not.
Amber is fossil tree resin, an organic material with no crystal lattice. That is why it is not a mineral.
The pictures show resin oozing from wood, rough pieces of amber and amber jewelry.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Synthetic minerals** are made by humans copying nature, such as a bismuth crystal made by people. Minerals must be created by natural processes.

Gems are prized for rarity, beauty, value, color and mystique, and well-formed symmetric crystals interact with light beautifully. Crystals do **not** have magic powers and do not affect health or mood.

boxes.text: Why are diamond and graphite so different if both are carbon? Same atoms, different packing and bonding. Diamond is a rigid 3-D network of strong bonds. Graphite is flat sheets with weak bonds between them, so the sheets glide past each other (it is also used as a lubricant).
Poly = many, morph = shape. Polymorphs are one recipe baked into different shapes. Isotopes: same element (same spot on the periodic table) but different neutron count.

Isotopes vs polymorphs (practice-midterm Q13). Isotopes = atoms of one element with different neutrons. Polymorphs = minerals with the same formula but different crystal structure. Diamond and graphite are polymorphs, not isotopes.

steps.title: Atoms as balls and bonds
bullets: Atoms can be drawn as tiny balls held in place by chemical bonds. How the atoms are packed and what kind of bonding holds them sets the mineral's properties.

In an ionic bond one atom gives an electron to another. Sodium loses one (Na+, a positive **cation**) and chlorine gains one (Cl-, a negative **anion**). They attract and lock into a cubic lattice: halite, NaCl (salt).
In a **covalent bond** atoms share electrons instead (O2, methane, the Si-O links in silicates).

steps.title: Order gives symmetry
bullets: The ordered atom arrangement gives crystals **symmetry**: a mirror plane splits a halite cube or a snowflake into matching halves.
The symmetry is diagnostic, which means it helps identify a mineral.
X-ray diffraction can reveal the order: X-rays hit a crystal and the diffracted beams make a dot pattern on a screen that reflects the atom arrangement.

steps.title: Diamond versus graphite
bullets: **Polymorphs** are minerals with the same chemical formula but different crystal structures. **Diamond and graphite** are both pure carbon.
Diamond has strong bonds in all directions, so it is the **hardest** mineral.
Graphite has strong bonds inside its layers but **weak bonds between layers**, so it is one of the softest.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Atoms have a nucleus of protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) with electrons (-) around it. The number of protons is the **atomic number** and defines the element.
**Isotopes** are the same element (same protons) with a **different number of neutrons**. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, carbon-13 has 7 neutrons, carbon-14 has 8.

sections.title: Crystal growth, shapes and the six crystal structures

boxes.text: Why is the interfacial angle constant? Because the outer faces are just the edges of the same repeating atom grid. A tiny crystal and a giant one have the same grid, so the angles match. The goniometer is the angle gauge.
Space = faces. A geode is an empty room: crystals can stretch out and show faces. A packed rock is a crowded bus: nobody gets a clean shape.
The 'why' answer is not shown; the sensible choice is packing in 3-D space (reasoning, not stated in the sources). Textbook 1 does not list the number of crystal systems.

bullets: Crystals come in many shapes and sizes: halite cube, diamond, staurolite, quartz, garnet, stibnite, calcite, kyanite.
The outside shape of a **euhedral** crystal (one with perfect faces) is a diagnostic property. It is controlled by how the atoms are arranged.
Bond strength can differ by direction. Barite grows faster in two directions and slower in one, which makes a flat, blocky **tabular** shape.

steps.title: Space gives faces
bullets: Crystals grow when atoms attach to the outside of an early crystal, which acts as a **seed**. As they grow they bump into each other.
Where there is open space, good crystal faces grow. Where growth is blocked, **no faces** form. An amethyst geode has perfect crystals because they grew into an open cavity.
**Euhedral** = perfect faces, **subhedral** = partly formed faces, anhedral = no faces because of crowding.

steps.title: A garnet crystal
bullets: This large garnet shows a diagnostic **dodecahedral** (12-sided) crystal habit.
It is **equant**: it has no long direction, so it is about the same size all around.
There are **six crystal structures**, drawn with axes: isometric, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic and hexagonal.
They differ in axis lengths and angles. Isometric has all axes equal at 90 degrees, while triclinic has all angles and lengths variable.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Atoms in a crystal are arranged in a specific geometric pattern, like construction **scaffolding** around a building.

**Law of Constancy of Interfacial Angles**: equivalent faces on two samples of the same mineral **always** meet at the same angle. For example, a quartz cross-section shows 120 degrees, measured with a goniometer.

boxes.text: Why does cooling or evaporating make crystals? Heat makes atoms vibrate. When a melt cools or water evaporates, ions are squeezed or slowed until they lock into a repeating pattern. Too much dissolved salt (saturation) forces them out of the water.
Salt in a sunny puddle: the water leaves, the salt stays. That is precipitation by evaporation.
'Freezing from a melt' means magma or lava cooling into rock crystals, not freezing water.

steps.title: Giant gypsum crystals
bullets: These gypsum crystals are the largest mineral crystals known. They grew by precipitation from **hot water** that once filled the cave.

**Precipitation**: ions dissolved in water come together and form solid crystals. This happens when the solution cools, when water evaporates, or when the chemistry changes, once the water is **saturated** (cannot hold more dissolved material).

steps.title: Ways minerals form
bullets: Minerals form by freezing from a melt, precipitation from solution or chemical reaction. Living things make **biogenic** minerals.
Another way to group them: precipitation from water, crystallization from magma, and precipitation by organisms.
By organisms: shells and bones. The most common mineral made this way is **calcite** (CaCO3), often as its polymorph **aragonite**, as in this mussel shell. Radiolaria make silica shells.

steps.title: Crystals crowd each other
bullets: As crystals grow they often run into other growing crystals. Where they have open space they grow good faces; where growth is blocked they do not.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Crystallization from magma**: magma (molten rock) cools, atoms slow down and lock into crystals. Lava is magma at the surface.
Evaporation examples: Great Salt Lake and Bonneville Salt Flats make halite.

boxes.text: Why is streak better than colour? Colour on the outside changes with impurities and weathering. Powdering the mineral shows the true colour of the mineral itself, which stays the same. Hematite can look black, silver or red but always streaks reddish-brown.
Streak = the mineral's 'signature' drawn on a plate. Colour = its 'outfit', which can change.

Practice-midterm Q16: two hematite samples with different colours but the same reddish-brown streak shows streak is MORE reliable than colour (not the other way round). Also, a mineral harder than the plate cannot give a streak.

steps.title: Identification is a skill
bullets: Identifying minerals is a **skill**. Some properties are obvious at a glance, others need handling or tests.
The physical properties that usually allow ready identification are color, streak, hardness, luster, specific gravity, crystal habit and cleavage (or lack of it).

steps.title: Color
bullets: **Color** is the part of visible light that is **not absorbed** by the mineral.
It is diagnostic for some minerals (malachite) and a poor indicator for others (quartz comes clear, milky or rose).
Color changes with impurities. Water makes quartz milky. Malachite is green and azurite blue because of copper.
**Streak** is the colour of the crushed powder a mineral leaves when rubbed on an **unglazed porcelain plate**. Hematite leaves a reddish-brown streak.
Streak only works for minerals with a hardness of less than about 6. Harder minerals scratch the plate instead.
Pyrite looks brassy gold but its streak is black to greenish-black.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Luster** is how a mineral surface scatters light. There are two main groups: **metallic** (looks like metal, e.g. pyrite) and nonmetallic.
Nonmetallic lusters: silky, vitreous (glassy), satiny, resinous, pearly, earthy (dull) and adamantine (brilliant). Feldspar is nonmetallic.

boxes.text: Why do stronger bonds mean a harder mineral? To scratch a mineral you must break its atom links. Stronger links resist the scratch. That is why diamond (strong bonds everywhere) is 10 and graphite (weak bonds between layers) is 1.
Order to learn: Talc, Gypsum, Calcite, Fluorite, Apatite, Orthoclase, Quartz, Topaz, Corundum, Diamond. Memory sentence: 'Tall Girls Can Flirt And Offer Quick Tips, Cool Dudes.'

Textbook calls steel pocketknife 5.5 and says it separates hard from soft minerals. Same number, so use 5.5. If a mineral scratches glass (5.5) but is scratched by quartz (7), it must be between 5.5 and 7: orthoclase (6), as in practice-midterm Q14. Topaz (8) is harder than quartz, so it cannot be the answer.

bullets: Hardness is the scratching resistance of a mineral, directly linked to **atomic-bond strength**. The **Mohs scale** runs from 1 to 10.
Everyday tools help: fingernail 2.5, copper penny 3.5, glass or steel knife 5.5, steel file 6.5.
The graph shows true hardness is not a straight line. Diamond (10) shoots far above corundum (9), roughly 3 to 4 times harder.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The harder mineral scratches the softer one. Scratch tests compare an unknown to known minerals or tools.

boxes.text: Why does mica peel in sheets? Inside each sheet the bonds are strong, but between the sheets the bonds are weak. The mineral splits along the weak planes. Quartz has strong bonds in every direction, so no weak plane exists and it fractures.
Cleavage = clean flat breaks, like peeling a sticker or snapping a chocolate bar along its grooves. Fracture = random, like breaking glass.

First-midterm Q10: the feature used to identify minerals is cleavage (not advantage, peerage, lineage or selvage). Also: cleavage is NOT the same as a crystal face. Cleavage goes right through the crystal; faces are only the outside.

steps.title: What cleavage is
bullets: **Cleavage** is the tendency of a mineral to break along **lattice planes with weaker atomic bonds**. It makes flat, shiny surfaces, sometimes in steps.
Cleavage is **throughgoing**: it repeats all through the crystal. Crystal faces are only on the outside surface.

steps.title: One or two directions
bullets: The number of cleavage planes and the angles between them are diagnostic.
One direction: **muscovite** (mica). Two directions at 90 degrees: **potassium feldspar**.
Two directions NOT at 90 degrees (about 60 and 120): amphibole.

steps.title: Three directions
bullets: **Three directions at 90 degrees**: halite, which breaks into cubes.

steps.title: No weak planes: fracture
bullets: Minerals with no planes of weakness (bonds equally strong in all directions) break by **fracture** instead of cleavage.
Obsidian and quartz show curved **conchoidal fracture**.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: More cleavage examples: pyroxene has 2 imperfect cleavages at about 90 degrees, amphibole 2 perfect ones at 60 and 120, calcite 3 at about 75, and galena and pyrite 3 at 90.

boxes.text: Why does calcite fizz? It is a carbonate (CaCO3). Acid attacks the carbonate and releases bubbles of gas, so acid is a quick field test for it.
Think of kitchen senses: tastes like salt = halite, smells like eggs = sulfur, sticks to a magnet = magnetite.

Practice-midterm Q17: white, hardness 3, three cleavages NOT at 90 degrees (rhombs), fizzes in dilute acid = calcite. Halite has cubic cleavage and tastes salty; gypsum is hardness 2 and does not fizz; quartz is hardness 7 with no cleavage.

bullets: Less common properties can help too: **effervescence** (fizzes in acid), **magnetism**, taste, smell, feel, elasticity, diaphaneity (transparency), piezoelectricity (charge when squeezed), pyroelectricity (charge when heated), refractive index, malleability (hammered into sheets), ductility (drawn into wires), sectility (shaved with a knife).
Examples: sulfur smells like rotten eggs, halite tastes like salt (it IS salt), magnetite is magnetic.
A drop of **dilute hydrochloric acid** fizzes on calcite. Dolomite fizzes only slowly, and only as a powder.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Other useful properties: specific gravity (density compared with water) and heft, fluorescence under UV light, and striations on plagioclase.

sections.title: Which elements make up Earth and the crust

boxes.text: Why do silicates rule the crust? Oxygen and silicon are the two most abundant crust elements (74.3% by weight), so the most common building block is a silicon-oxygen unit, the silica tetrahedron.
Crust: O then Si (rhymes with 'Oh, Si!'), then Al, Fe, Ca, Na, K, Mg. Whole Earth swaps in iron.
Do not mix up the two charts.

steps.title: Elements in the Solar System
bullets: This graph shows how common each element is in the Solar System by atom count (silicon is the reference). Light elements like H and He are most common, and the numbers fall off for heavy elements.
It is background only: the next charts focus on Earth.
The **crust** is mostly **8 elements**. Oxygen and silicon together are 74.3% by weight.
By weight: O 46.6, Si 27.7, Al 8.1, Fe 5, Ca 3.6, Na 2.8, K 2.6, Mg 2.1.
By atoms oxygen is 60.5% and silicon 20.5%. By volume oxygen is 93.8%: oxygen ions are big and take up almost all the space.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The **whole Earth** by mass is dominated by **iron and oxygen**: Iron 32.1%, Oxygen 30.1%, Silicon 15.1%, Magnesium 13.9%, Other 8.8%.
That is why **silicate minerals** (silicon + oxygen) dominate the crust.

sections.title: Silica tetrahedron and the silicate structures

head: Structure
Oxygens shared
Examples
Cleavage link
rows: No planes of weakness: no cleavage (olivine)
Quartz: none, conchoidal fracture. Feldspar: 2 cleavages at 90

boxes.text: Why does structure control cleavage? Cleavage follows planes where bonds are weakest. In a sheet silicate the bonds BETWEEN sheets are weak, so mica splits in one direction. In quartz every bond is a strong Si-O link in all directions, so there is no weak plane: no cleavage, just curved fracture. Chains are bonded to each other by weaker cation links, giving two cleavage directions.

Think of sharing: Isolated = no sharing (loners), Chain = hold hands in a line, Double chain = two lines linked, Sheet = a flat net, Framework = a full 3-D jungle gym. More sharing means a more tightly locked crystal.

Ratios disagree between sources. Textbook 3.3.4 says sheet silicates have Si:O of 2:5 (Si4O10), and its amphibole formula (RSi4O11)2 implies 4:11 for double chains. Single chain 1:3 and framework 1:2 agree everywhere. Also: practice-midterm Q15 answer is 'framework silicate with strong Si-O bonds equally in all directions'.

steps.title: Single chain
bullets: In a **single chain** silicate, two of the three basal oxygens of each tetrahedron are bonded to neighbours. The Si:O ratio is **1:3**.
Pyroxene (augite) is the example.

steps.title: Double chain
bullets: A **double chain** is like two single chains that share oxygens where the tetrahedra touch. The Si:O ratio is **2:7**.
Amphibole (hornblende) is the example.

steps.title: Framework
bullets: In a **framework** silicate all oxygens are shared, forming a 3-D network. Si:O is **1:2**.
Quartz (SiO2) and the feldspars are examples: orthoclase KAlSi3O8, albite NaAlSi3O8, anorthite CaAl2Si2O8.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The basic building block is the **SiO4 (4-) silica tetrahedron**: one silicon in the middle with four oxygens at the corners (a pyramid with 4 faces). The small silicon sits in the gap between four big oxygens. Only part of each corner oxygen's charge is used up, so the corners can link to other tetrahedra or to cations (Al, Fe, Mg, K, Na, Ca).

Silicates are divided into classes by how the tetrahedra share oxygens. In **isolated tetrahedra** none are shared and cations hold them together (olivine, garnet; pyrope is Mg3Al2(SiO4)3). In a **sheet**, oxygens are shared along the base but not the top one, so Si:O is 4:11 (micas such as muscovite, and clays).

boxes.text: Why is quartz so common in sand and sandstone? It is very resistant to weathering, so other minerals break down and quartz grains survive.
Felsic = Feldspar + Silica (light colour, continental). Mafic = Magnesium + Fe (iron), dark.
Diamond is a pure carbon mineral. Amber is the non-mineral.

steps.title: Pyroxene
bullets: Pyroxene is a dark, iron- and magnesium-rich (**ferromagnesian**) mineral and a common single-chain silicate.
Two pyroxenes named here are augite and clinoenstatite (MgSiO3).

steps.title: Amphibole
bullets: Amphiboles such as hornblende are dark ferromagnesian minerals too, and important double-chain silicates.
Named examples include hornblende and tremolite-actinolite.

steps.title: Non-silicate minerals
bullets: Not all minerals are silicates. Other groups: sulfides (galena, pyrite), sulphates (gypsum), oxides (hematite, magnetite), halides (halite), carbonates (calcite, dolomite) and phosphates (apatite).
Carbonates and halides often form from evaporation or by organisms. **Native elements** like gold are pure.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Feldspar** is the single most abundant mineral in the crust (about 50%); **quartz** is the most abundant at the surface because it resists weathering.

Rock-forming silicates: felsic quartz and K-feldspar (framework silicates) and plagioclase (a Ca-Na feldspar, albite to anorthite series); dark ferromagnesian olivine (Fe,Mg)2SiO4 (green, from the mantle), pyroxene and amphibole; micas (dark biotite, light muscovite); and clays, which form from weathering of rocks.

quiz.q: A silica tetrahedron is composed of which atoms?
quiz.why: SiO4: one silicon in the middle with four oxygens at the corners.

quiz.q: Which of the following is not a mineral?
quiz.why: Amber is fossil tree resin (organic, no crystal structure). The others are natural crystalline solids.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a mineral?
quiz.why: Obsidian is volcanic glass: its atoms have no repeating pattern, so it is not crystalline.

quiz.q: How many possible crystal structures exist?
quiz.why: There are six crystal structures: isometric, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal.

quiz.q: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon but have different crystal structures. What are they?
quiz.why: Same formula but different crystal structure means polymorphs. Isotopes differ in neutron number, not structure.

quiz.q: An unknown mineral scratches window glass (hardness about 5.5) but is scratched by quartz. Which mineral could it be?
quiz.why: It must be harder than 5.5 but softer than quartz (7). Orthoclase is 6. Topaz (8) is harder than quartz.

quiz.q: Why does quartz have no cleavage?
options: It is a sheet silicate with weak bonds between the sheets
It is a framework silicate with strong Si-O bonds equally in all directions
It has no silicon in it
It is too soft to break cleanly
quiz.why: No plane of weaker bonds exists, so it fractures (conchoidal) instead of cleaving. Quartz is SiO2, a framework silicate.

quiz.q: One hematite sample is black and another is red, but both leave a reddish-brown line on a porcelain plate. What does this show?
options: Colour is the most reliable identification property
Streak is more reliable than colour for identification
Both samples are actually different minerals
quiz.why: Colour changes between samples but the powder (streak) stays constant. Hematite always streaks reddish-brown.

quiz.q: A white mineral has hardness 3, breaks into rhomb-shaped pieces (three cleavage directions NOT at 90 degrees), and fizzes in dilute acid. What is it?
quiz.why: Calcite is hardness 3 (Mohs), has three cleavages not at 90 degrees (rhombs) and effervesces in acid. Halite has cubic cleavage.

quiz.q: Minerals can be identified by various properties including colour and hardness. Which of the following is a feature also used to help identify minerals?
quiz.why: Cleavage is how a mineral breaks along flat planes. It is one of the standard identification properties.

quiz.q: Which statements about a mineral are correct? I. It is naturally occurring. II. It must be made by a living organism. III. It has a repeating (crystalline) atom arrangement.
quiz.why: I and III are in the definition. II is false: biogenic minerals are only a special case; most form by geologic processes.

quiz.q: Which statements about silicate structures are correct? I. Framework silicates have a Si:O ratio of 1:3. II. Isolated tetrahedra do not share any oxygens. III. In single-chain silicates two of the three basal oxygens are bonded together.
quiz.why: Framework is 1:2 (single chain is 1:3), so I is wrong. II and III are correct.

quiz.q: Which statement about hardness is INCORRECT?
options: Hardness is scratching resistance linked to atomic-bond strength.
A copper penny (3.5) can scratch calcite (3).
The Mohs scale runs from 1 to 10.
quiz.why: A harder mineral scratches a softer one. Calcite is softer than fluorite, so it cannot scratch it.

quiz.q: A mineral can be scratched by your fingernail (2.5). Which of these could it be?
quiz.why: It must be softer than 2.5. Gypsum is 2. The others are 5 or higher.

quiz.q: A mineral scratches a copper penny (3.5) but is scratched by a steel knife blade (5.5). Which could it be?
quiz.why: Its hardness is between 3.5 and 5.5. Fluorite is 4. Talc, gypsum and calcite are 3 or lower; corundum is 9.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Why does mica peel apart into thin sheets?
options: It has strong bonds in every direction
Bonds between the sheets are much weaker than bonds within the sheets
quiz.why: Mica is a sheet silicate. Weak bonds between sheets make one perfect cleavage direction.

quiz.q: How can you tell a cleavage plane from a crystal face?
options: Cleavage is throughgoing; crystal faces are on the outside surface only
Crystal faces are throughgoing; cleavage is on the outside only
quiz.why: Cleavage repeats through the crystal; faces are only on external surfaces.

quiz.q: The Earth's crust is composed mostly of 8 elements. What percent by weight do oxygen (46.6%) and silicon (27.7%) make up together?
Which two elements dominate the mass of the ENTIRE Earth (not just the crust)?
quiz.why: Iron 32.1% and Oxygen 30.1%. In the crust, oxygen and silicon dominate.

quiz.q: Calcite breaks into rhomb-shaped pieces. Which describes its cleavage?
quiz.why: Calcite has three directions not at 90 degrees. Halite is the three-at-90 example.

quiz.q: Which statements about special mineral properties are correct? I. Magnetite is magnetic. II. Halite tastes like salt. III. Sulfur smells like rotten eggs.
quiz.why: All three are standard examples of special properties.

quiz.q: The giant gypsum crystals in a cave grew by:
options: precipitation from hot water that once filled the cave
quiz.why: They grew by precipitation from hot water that previously filled the cave.

quiz.q: Which mineral shows two cleavage directions that are NOT at 90 degrees?
quiz.why: Amphibole has two cleavages that are not at 90 degrees (about 60 and 120). K-feldspar has two at 90, muscovite one, halite three at 90, quartz none.

quiz.q: Reasoning: A mineral has bonds that are equally strong in all directions. What happens when it breaks?
options: It cleaves in three directions at 90 degrees
It breaks along a single flat plane
quiz.why: With no planes of weakness it fractures (e.g. conchoidal), as obsidian and quartz do.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Diamond is the hardest mineral and graphite one of the softest, yet both are pure carbon. Why?
options: They have different isotopes of carbon
Different atomic bonding and structure: strong bonds all around in diamond, weak bonds between layers in graphite
quiz.why: They are polymorphs. The type of bonding controls hardness.
